p.src: When Baoyu saw that Qingwen had finished mending the peacock-feather cloak, utterly exhausting her strength and endangering her health, he hurriedly told a young maid to come and massage her. After taking turns massaging each other for a while, they lay down to rest. Before the time needed to eat a meal had passed, broad daylight had come. Baoyu did not go out, but ordered that a physician be summoned at once. Presently Imperial Physician Wang arrived. After taking her pulse, he said in puzzlement, “She was somewhat better yesterday, so why has her pulse become weak, faint, floating, and contracted today? Could she have eaten too much? If not, she must have overtaxed her mind. The external infection has cleared, but neglecting proper care after perspiration is no trifling matter.” As he spoke, he went out to write a prescription and then brought it in. When Baoyu examined it, he saw that the dispersing medicines for expelling pathogenic influences had been reduced, while restorative ingredients for nourishing the spirits and blood—such as poria, rehmannia root, and Chinese angelica—had been added. Baoyu hurriedly ordered someone to decoct the medicine, sighing meanwhile, “What am I to do? If anything should happen to her, the guilt will be mine alone.” Lying on her pillow, Qingwen exclaimed, “Oh, my dear young master! Go and attend to your own affairs. It is hardly as though I have consumption!” Baoyu had no choice but to leave. By the latter half of the day, however, he returned, saying that he felt unwell. Although Qingwen’s illness was serious, fortunately she had always been one to exert her body rather than trouble her mind; moreover, her customary diet was plain and temperate, so neither hunger nor satiety had harmed her. The Jia household had a customary secret remedy observed by masters and servants alike: at the least sign of a cold or cough, complete fasting came first, and medicine and restorative care second. Thus, when she first fell ill a few days earlier, she had fasted completely for two or three days and taken her medicine with great care. Now, after overexerting herself a little, she received twice the usual nourishment and care for several more days and gradually recovered. Of late, the young ladies in the garden had all been taking their meals in their own rooms, which made the cooking and serving more convenient. Baoyu himself found various ways to order soups and broths for Qingwen and regulate her diet, but there is no need to relate the details.

p.src: After seeing her mother buried, Xiren had already returned. Sheyue duly reported to Baoyu everything Ping’er had said about Nanny Song and Zhui’er, as well as how Qingwen had driven Zhui’er out. Xiren said nothing else, merely remarking that Qingwen had been a little too hasty. Li Wan, too, had caught a seasonal cold; Lady Xing was suffering from severely inflamed eyes, and Yingchun and Xiuyan had gone to nurse her and administer her medicine morning and evening; Aunt Li’s younger brother had taken Aunt Li, Li Wen, and Li Qi home to stay for several days; and Baoyu saw that Xiren often grieved for her mother while Qingwen had still not fully recovered. p.src: Presently Jia Zhen came in for his meal, and Jia Rong’s wife withdrew. Jia Zhen asked Madam You, “Have we collected the imperial grant for the spring sacrifice yet?” Madam You replied, “I sent Rong’er to collect it today.” Jia Zhen said, “Our family may have no need of these few taels of silver, but they are nevertheless a token of His Majesty’s heavenly favor. It should be collected early, shown to the Old Lady in the other mansion, and used to purchase offerings for our ancestors. Thus we receive the Emperor’s favor from above and enjoy our ancestors’ blessings from below. Even if we spent ten thousand taels on offerings to our ancestors, it could never be as honorable as this, nor would it carry both imperial grace and auspicious blessing. Apart from one or two families like ours, what could those impoverished hereditary officials offer their ancestors for the New Year if they did not depend on this silver? The Emperor’s bounty is truly boundless; His Majesty has considered everything.” “Exactly so,” said Madam You.

p.src: While the two were still talking, a servant came to report, “The young master has returned.” Jia Zhen ordered that he be shown in. Jia Rong entered carrying a small yellow cloth pouch in both hands. Jia Zhen asked, “Why did it take you the whole day?” Jia Rong replied with an ingratiating smile, “Today the grant was not issued at the Ministry of Rites; its distribution had been assigned to the storehouse of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, so I had to go there before I could collect it. The officials there all sent their regards to you, Father. They said they had not seen you for a long time and missed you greatly.” Jia Zhen laughed. “It is not me they miss. With the New Year approaching, what they miss is either my presents or the theatricals and wine I provide.” As he spoke, he examined the yellow cloth pouch. Stamped upon it were the four large characters “Imperial Favor Forever Bestowed”; on the other side was the seal of the Department of Sacrificial Worship under the Ministry of Rites. A line of smaller characters read: “Two perpetual spring-sacrifice grants imperially bestowed upon Jia Yan, Duke of Ning, and Jia Yuan, Duke of Rong, commuted to a net sum of so many taels of silver. On such-and-such a date, month, and year, Jia Rong, Captain of the Imperial Guard and expectant palace guard, received the same in person before the court. Duty assistant director of the Court: So-and-so.” Beneath this was a vermilion signature flourish.

p.src: Jia Zhen ordered that he be brought in. Presently Wu Jinxiao came in and remained in the courtyard, where he kowtowed and paid his respects. Jia Zhen had someone pull him to his feet and said with a smile, “You are still hale and hearty.” Wu Jinxiao replied with a smile, “Thanks to your blessing, Master, I can still get about.” Jia Zhen said, “Your son is grown now. You might as well let him make the journey.” Wu Jinxiao smiled. “To tell you the truth, Master, we older fellows are accustomed to the journey and would feel restless if we did not come. And are not all the young ones eager to come and see something of life beneath the Son of Heaven’s feet? But they are young after all, and I fear some mishap on the road. In another few years I shall be able to trust them with it.” Jia Zhen asked, “How many days have you been on the road?” Wu Jinxiao replied, “Master, the snow has been heavy this year, four or five feet deep everywhere outside. The day before yesterday it suddenly turned warm and began to thaw, making the roads extremely difficult, so I was delayed for several days. Though the journey took a month and two days, I knew the date was near and feared you would grow anxious, so I hurried here as fast as I could.” Jia Zhen said, “That explains why you have arrived only today. I have just looked at the list. You old rogue have come to challenge me to a contest again this year.” Wu Jinxiao hurried two steps forward and replied, “Master, the harvest truly was poor this year. From the time the rains began in March until August, they continued without a break, and we never had as many as five clear days in succession. Then in September, hailstones as large as bowls fell across nearly thirteen hundred li, injuring or destroying people, houses, livestock, and crops by the thousands and tens of thousands. That is why the returns are like this. I would never dare lie to you.” Jia Zhen frowned. “I had reckoned that you would bring at least five thousand taels of silver. What use is this little amount? Between you, there are only eight or nine estates left now. This year two have already reported droughts or floods, and now you come challenging me like this. You truly mean to stop us from celebrating the New Year!” Wu Jinxiao said, “Your lands have actually fared comparatively well, Master! My brother’s place is only a little over a hundred li from mine, yet who would have thought conditions there could be so much worse? He now manages eight estates belonging to the other house, several times as much land as you have here. Yet this year he has brought only about the same amount of produce, with no more than two or three thousand additional taels of silver, and even that was scraped together amid famine and hardship.” Jia Zhen said, “Quite so. Things are manageable on my side. There are no great extraordinary expenses; it is only the year’s ordinary outlay that costs so much. If I put up with a little inconvenience, I can economize somewhat. As for the customary annual gifts and invitations, if I am thick-skinned enough, I can cut back on those too, and that will settle it. But the other house is different. In recent years it has acquired many new expenses that simply cannot be avoided, yet neither its income nor its property has increased at all. During the past year or two they have actually lost a great deal. If we do not ask you people for it, whom else can we ask?”

p.src: Wu Jinxiao laughed. “Though that household has taken on new expenses, money comes in as well as goes out. Surely Her Highness and His Majesty bestow rewards upon you!” Hearing this, Jia Zhen laughed and said to Jia Rong and the others, “Listen to him! Isn’t that absurd?” Jia Rong and the others hastened to laugh. “How could people from remote mountain hollows and coastal backwaters understand such matters? Do you imagine Her Highness has handed the imperial treasury over to us? Even if she wished to, the decision would not be hers to make. Of course rewards are bestowed. But at the customary seasons and festivals, they amount to no more than colored silks, antiques, and trinkets. Even when money is given, it is no more than a hundred taels of gold, worth only a thousand taels of silver. What use is that over an entire year? In each of these past two years, haven’t we lost several thousand taels more than we received? Just reckon how much was spent the first year on the imperial visit and the building of the garden, and you will understand. If there is another imperial visit in two years, I fear we shall be utterly ruined.” Jia Zhen laughed. “That is why honest country folk like them see only the outward show and know nothing of what lies beneath. It is like making a chime-hammer from corkwood—fine to look at outside, bitter within.” Jia Rong laughed again and said to Jia Zhen, “That household truly is poor. p.src: All were inscriptions in the imperial hand. Within, incense and candles blazed amid brocade hangings and embroidered curtains; though the ancestral tablets stood arrayed there, they could not be seen distinctly. The members of the Jia clan took their appointed places according to senior and junior branches: Jia Jing officiated, Jia She assisted, Jia Zhen presented the wine cups, Jia Lian and Jia Cong offered the silk, Baoyu held the incense, while Jia Chang and Jia Ling spread the prayer mats and attended the brazier for burnt offerings. The musicians in blue played; the wine was offered three times, and when the bows and risings were complete, the silk was burned and wine poured in libation. The ceremony ended, the music ceased, and all withdrew. Everyone then surrounded and followed Grandmother Jia into the main hall, where brocade curtains hung high before the portraits, colored screens sheltered them, and incense and candles shone brilliantly. In the center above hung portraits of the two founders of the Ning and Rong houses, both wearing robes embroidered with dragons and jade girdles; on either side hung several more scroll portraits of their forebears. Jia Xing, Jia Zhi, and the others stood at intervals from the inner ceremonial gate as far as the veranda of the main hall. Jia Jing and Jia She stood outside the threshold, while the women of the family stood within. All the household servants and pages remained outside the ceremonial gate. Whenever a dish arrived, it was passed to the ceremonial gate, where Jia Xing, Jia Zhi, and the others received it and relayed it in order to Jia Jing at the top of the steps. As Jia Rong was the eldest grandson of the senior branch, he alone stood within the threshold among the women. Each dish carried in by Jia Jing was passed to Jia Rong, who handed it to his wife; from her it went through Xifeng, Madam You, and the others until, on reaching the offering table, it was passed to Lady Wang. Lady Wang passed it to Grandmother Jia, who then lifted it onto the table. Lady Xing stood west of the offering table facing east and placed the offerings together with Grandmother Jia. Only after all the dishes, rice, soup, pastries, wine, and tea had been passed forward did Jia Rong withdraw down the steps and take his place at the head of the rank occupied by Jia Qin. Of those whose names contained the literary radical, Jia Jing stood first; below them came those with the jade radical, headed by Jia Zhen; and below them those with the grass radical, headed by Jia Rong. The senior branches stood on the left and the junior on the right, the men to the east and the women to the west. When Grandmother Jia took incense and bowed, everyone knelt together, filling the five-bay great hall, the three-bay front annex, the inner and outer verandas and eaves, and both courtyards above and below the steps with a splendid profusion that left not an inch of open ground. Not a whisper could be heard—only the faint chiming and tinkling of golden bells and jade pendants as they swayed, mingled with the rustle and shuffle of boots and shoes as everyone knelt and rose. When the ceremony was over, Jia Jing, Jia She, and the others hurriedly withdrew and went to the Rong Mansion, there to await Grandmother Jia and pay their respects to her.

p.src: The floor of Madam You’s principal room had already been covered throughout with red felt. In the center stood a large gilded enamel brazier with three elephant-trunk legs and a loach-rimmed edge. The kang facing the room was spread with new scarlet felt and furnished with a bright-red embroidered backrest and bolster showing cloud-wreathed dragons presenting the emblem of longevity; over these lay a black fox-fur coverlet and a great white fox-fur seat cushion, upon which Grandmother Jia was invited to sit. Fur cushions had also been laid on either side for two or three sisters-in-law of Grandmother Jia’s generation. Fur cushions were likewise spread on the small kang behind the transverse screen at this end for Lady Xing and the others. On the floor, twelve carved-lacquer chairs faced one another in two rows, each fitted with an identical gray-squirrel chair cover and small cushion, with a large brass foot-warmer beneath it; Baoqin and the other young ladies were seated there. Madam You personally carried tea to Grandmother Jia on a tray, while Jia Rong’s wife served the elderly ladies. Madam You then served Lady Xing and the others, and Jia Rong’s wife served the young ladies. Xifeng, Li Wan, and the others remained standing on the floor to attend them. When tea was finished, Lady Xing and the others rose first to attend Grandmother Jia. Grandmother Jia drank her tea and exchanged a few casual words with her elderly sisters-in-law, then ordered them to see whether her sedan chair was ready. Xifeng hurried forward to help her up. Madam You said with a smile, “We have already prepared your evening meal, dear Old Lady. Every year you refuse to do us the honor of dining here before you leave. Can it really be that we are no match for that girl Xifeng?” Supporting Grandmother Jia by the arm, Xifeng laughed and said, “Hurry along, Old Ancestress. Let’s go home for dinner and pay no attention to her.” Grandmother Jia laughed. “With the ancestors enshrined here, you are already rushed off your feet. How could you possibly have me adding to the commotion? Besides, even though I never dine here, every year you send food over to me anyway. You may as well send it over again. Whatever I cannot finish I can save for tomorrow, and then I shall get to eat even more of it.” Her words made everyone laugh. She further instructed Madam You, “Be sure to appoint reliable people to tend the incense and candles during the night. This is not something to be treated carelessly.” Madam You assented. As they spoke, they came outside to the front of the warm pavilion, where Grandmother Jia entered her sedan chair. Madam You and the other women withdrew behind the screen; only then did the pages bring in the bearers and have the sedan carried out through the main gate. Madam You also accompanied Lady Xing and the others to the Rong Mansion.

p.src: The sedan chairs passed through the main gate. Along the entire eastern side of the street stood the ceremonial insignia, attendants, and musical instruments of the Duke of Ning, while along the western side stood those of the Duke of Rong; all passersby had been cleared away and were forbidden to use the street. Before long they reached the Rong Mansion, where every doorway from the main gate through the principal halls had likewise been opened in a straight line. This time they did not alight below the warm pavilion. They passed the great hall, turned west, and dismounted before the main hall in Grandmother Jia's quarters. Surrounded by the others, Grandmother Jia proceeded to her principal apartment, which also gleamed as if new with brocade carpets and embroidered screens. In the brazier at the center of the room, fragrant pine, cypress, and lily herb were burning. Once Grandmother Jia had taken her seat, an old serving-woman came to report, “The venerable ladies have come to pay their respects.” Grandmother Jia hurriedly rose to welcome them, but two or three of her elderly sisters-in-law had already entered. They clasped one another's hands, exchanged smiles for a while, and repeatedly deferred to one another. After they had taken tea and departed, Grandmother Jia escorted them only as far as the inner ceremonial gate, then returned and resumed her place of honor. Jia Jing, Jia She, and the others entered at the head of the younger men of the clan. Grandmother Jia said with a smile, “You have all had a hard time of it throughout the year. Never mind the formal salutations.” Even as she spoke, however, the men in one group and the women in another came forward group by group and duly performed their salutations. Armchairs were then placed on either side, and the elders took their seats in order of seniority to receive the salutations of those below them. The men and women, pages and maids of both mansions likewise paid their respects in groups according to the rank of their duties. New Year's money, purses, and little gold and silver ingots were distributed, and the reunion feast was laid out. The men sat in the east and the women in the west. After tusu wine, reunion soup, auspicious fruits, and wish-fulfilling cakes had been presented, Grandmother Jia rose and went into the inner room to change, whereupon everyone dispersed. That night incense was burned and offerings were made in every Buddhist shrine and before every Kitchen God. In the courtyard of Lady Wang's main apartments stood paper images of Heaven and Earth with incense and offerings; great horn lanterns were also hung in two brilliantly lit rows over the main gate of Prospect Garden, while pathway lanterns shone everywhere. Masters and servants alike were dressed in dazzling finery. All night long the bustle of voices and the clamor of talk and laughter filled the air, while firecrackers and fireworks went off without cease. At the fifth watch the next morning, Grandmother Jia and the others again donned full court dress appropriate to their ranks and, preceded by a complete ceremonial retinue, entered the palace to offer New Year's congratulations and to wish Yuanchun longevity. After returning from the palace banquet, they went to the Ning Mansion to sacrifice to the successive generations of ancestors. Only then did they come home, receive the formal salutations, change their clothes, and rest. Grandmother Jia declined to receive any of the relatives and friends who came with holiday greetings. She spoke at leisure only with Aunt Xue and Aunt Li, or amused herself by playing games of go or cards with Baoyu, Baoqin, Baochai, Daiyu, and the other girls. Lady Wang and Xifeng were busy every day entertaining guests at New Year's feasts. The halls and courtyards on their side were continually filled with theatricals and banquets, and relatives and friends came in an unbroken stream; it was seven or eight days before the bustle ended. Soon the Lantern Festival was approaching, and both the Ning and Rong mansions were decked with lanterns and colored decorations. On the eleventh, Jia She entertained Grandmother Jia and the others; the following day Jia Zhen gave another feast. Grandmother Jia attended both and stayed informally for half a day.

The men and women, pages and maids of both mansions likewise paid their respects in groups according to the rank of their duties. New Year's money, purses, and little gold and silver ingots were distributed, and the reunion feast was laid out.

The men sat in the east and the women in the west. After tusu wine, reunion soup, auspicious fruits, and wish-fulfilling cakes had been presented, Grandmother Jia rose and went into the inner room to change, whereupon everyone dispersed.

That night incense was burned and offerings were made in every Buddhist shrine and before every Kitchen God. In the courtyard of Lady Wang's main apartments stood paper images of Heaven and Earth with incense and offerings; great horn lanterns were also hung in two brilliantly lit rows over the main gate of Prospect Garden, while pathway lanterns shone everywhere.

Masters and servants alike were dressed in dazzling finery. All night long the bustle of voices and the clamor of talk and laughter filled the air, while firecrackers and fireworks went off without cease.

At the fifth watch the next morning, Grandmother Jia and the others again donned full court dress appropriate to their ranks and, preceded by a complete ceremonial retinue, entered the palace to offer New Year's congratulations and to wish Yuanchun longevity.

After returning from the palace banquet, they went to the Ning Mansion to sacrifice to the successive generations of ancestors. Only then did they come home, receive the formal salutations, change their clothes, and rest.

Grandmother Jia declined to receive any of the relatives and friends who came with holiday greetings. She spoke at leisure only with Aunt Xue and Aunt Li, or amused herself by playing games of go or cards with Baoyu, Baoqin, Baochai, Daiyu, and the other girls.

Lady Wang and Xifeng were busy every day entertaining guests at New Year's feasts. The halls and courtyards on their side were continually filled with theatricals and banquets, and relatives and friends came in an unbroken stream; it was seven or eight days before the bustle ended.
Soon the Lantern Festival was approaching, and both the Ning and Rong mansions were decked with lanterns and colored decorations.
On the eleventh, Jia She entertained Grandmother Jia and the others; the following day Jia Zhen gave another feast. Grandmother Jia attended both and stayed informally for half a day.

p.src: Day after day, Lady Wang and Xifeng were themselves invited out to New Year's feasts more times than could be counted. On the evening of the fifteenth, Grandmother Jia ordered several tables of wine to be set in the great flower hall, engaged a small theatrical troupe, and had fine lanterns of every kind hung throughout. She then held a family banquet for the sons, nephews, grandsons, grandsons' wives, and other descendants of the Rong and Ning mansions. Jia Jing never drank wine, so he was not invited. On the seventeenth, once the ancestral rites were completed, he left the city again to pursue his spiritual cultivation. Even during the few days he spent at home, he remained alone and silent in a purified chamber, hearing and concerning himself with nothing; there is no more to be said of him here. Jia She partook briefly of Grandmother Jia's hospitality, then took his leave. Grandmother Jia knew that his presence made things awkward for them both, so she let him go as he wished. Back at his own residence, Jia She admired the lanterns and drank with his retainers. Naturally, the music of pipes and songs deafened the ear and rich brocades dazzled the eye; the carefree pleasures there were of quite a different kind from those on Grandmother Jia's side.

p.src: Meanwhile, some ten tables had been laid in Grandmother Jia's flower hall. Beside each table stood a small side table bearing the customary set of three incense utensils—a burner, a vase, and a box—and in the burner smoldered imperial palace incense scented with lilies. There were also little tray landscapes, about eight inches long, four or five inches wide, and two or three inches high, adorned with miniature rocks covered in moss and planted entirely with fresh flowers. There were small foreign-lacquer tea trays as well, holding cups from old kilns and assorted little tea pots in which the finest celebrated teas had been brewed. All the hanging ornaments were uniformly framed in openwork red sandalwood and inset with crimson gauze, on which flowers and poems in cursive script had been embroidered in openwork. It turned out that the woman who had embroidered these ornaments was a native of Gusu named Huiniang. She too came from a scholarly official family and was accomplished in calligraphy and painting. She embroidered one or two pieces only occasionally for her own amusement; they were never made for sale. All the flowers embroidered on these panels were modeled on sprays painted by famous masters of the Tang, Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties. Their designs and colors were therefore unfailingly elegant and could not be compared with the gaudy work of ordinary craftsmen. Beside every spray appeared an old line composed upon that flower by some writer of antiquity, whether from a poem, lyric, song, or rhapsody. Each was embroidered in cursive script with black floss, and the hooks and upward strokes, turns and angles, light and heavy touches, joined and broken lines were indistinguishable from brush-written cursive. They bore no resemblance to the stiff, forced, and offensive lettering of commercial embroidery. Since she did not use her skill for profit, her work, though known throughout the realm, was possessed by very few. Even among official and wealthy families, many had none of it. It came to be called “Hui Embroidery.” Of late, however, vulgar profiteers had begun imitating her needlework and making money by deceiving fools. Unhappily, Huiniang's life was short: she died at eighteen, and now not a single new piece could ever be obtained. Any family fortunate enough to own even one or two pieces kept them stored away as treasures and never used them. A band of literary pedants from the Hanlin Academy, deeply admiring the excellence of “Hui Embroidery,” declared that the word “embroidery” could not encompass its subtlety and that to apply it to such calligraphy was almost an affront. After conferring, they suppressed the word “embroidery” and replaced it with “pattern”; hence the work is now called “Hui Pattern.” A single genuine piece of “Hui Pattern” was therefore beyond price. For all the Jia family's splendor, it had possessed only two or three such pieces. Two had been presented to the throne the previous year, leaving only this one set of sixteen hanging panels. Grandmother Jia treasured them dearly and never included them among the various decorations displayed when entertaining guests, but kept them in her own quarters to admire whenever she felt inclined to give a banquet. Small vases from various old kilns were also adorned with fresh flowers and greenery arranged in such auspicious designs as “The Three Friends of Winter” and “Jade Hall Wealth and Honor.”

p.src: At the two tables above them sat Aunt Li and Aunt Xue. On the eastern side, a low, short-legged couch had been arranged for Grandmother Jia, complete with an openwork screen carved with kui-dragons, a backrest, a bolster, and a fur coverlet. At one end of the couch stood a very dainty little foreign-lacquered table decorated in gold, bearing a tea kettle, teacups, a rinsing bowl, foreign towels, and the like, as well as a spectacle case. Grandmother Jia reclined on the couch, chatting and laughing with the others for a while; then she took up her spectacles to peer at the stage before smiling at Aunt Xue and Aunt Li. “You must forgive me. I am old and my bones ache, so pardon my lack of ceremony and let me entertain you lying down.” She then ordered Amber to sit on the couch and pound her legs with a padded beauty's-fist mallet. No banquet table was placed below the couch; there was only a tall stand displaying a beaded ornament, a vase, an incense burner, and similar objects. Beside it stood another exquisite little high table set with winecups, spoons, and chopsticks. Her own banquet place was arranged beside the couch, and Baoqin, Xiangyun, Daiyu, and Baoyu were told to sit there. Whenever a dish or fruit was brought in, it was first presented to Grandmother Jia for inspection. If it pleased her, it was left on the little table for her to taste; then it was removed and placed at the four young people's table, so that they were regarded as sharing Grandmother Jia's place. Only below them, therefore, came the places of Lady Xing and Lady Wang, followed by You-shi, Li Wan, Xifeng, and Jia Rong's wife. Along the western side sat Baochai, Li Wen, Li Qi, Xiuyan, Yingchun and her sisters, and the others. From the great beams on either side hung a pair of clustered glass lotus lanterns—three lights in one cluster and five in the other—adorned with colored tassels. Before each table stood a lacquered stem supporting a downward-curving lotus leaf, on which a candle socket held a colored candle. The lotus leaves were made of chiseled enamel, and their movable fittings could be turned. They had now all been turned outward, shielding the light and directing it entirely toward the stage, so that the performance could be seen with exceptional clarity. The window lattices and doors had all been removed, and colored-tasselled palace lanterns of every kind hung in their place. Inside and outside the veranda eaves, and beneath the awnings over the covered walks on both sides, lanterns of every description crowded the space: horn, glass, pierced gauze, and spun-glass lanterns, embroidered, painted, appliquéd, carved, or made of silk or paper. The tables on the veranda were occupied by Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Jia Huan, Jia Cong, Jia Rong, Jia Qin, Jia Yun, Jia Ling, Jia Chang, and the others.

p.src: Grandmother Jia had also sent invitations to all the men and women of the clan. Some, however, were elderly and had no taste for bustling festivities; some could not conveniently leave because there was no one to look after their homes; some were beset by illness and could not come despite wishing to; some stayed away out of envy of the rich and shame at their own poverty; some even refused in a fit of pique because they disliked and feared Xifeng; while others were shy and awkward, unused to company and afraid to appear. Thus, numerous though the clan was, the only female guest who came was Lou-shi, Jia Jun's mother, who brought Jia Jun with her; and the only men who came were Jia Qin, Jia Yun, Jia Chang, and Jia Ling, the four who were then working under Xifeng. Though the company was therefore incomplete, it was still a lively gathering by the standards of a small family banquet. Presently, Lin Zhixiao's wife arrived with six married maids carrying three low kang tables. Each was covered with a strip of red felt on which lay newly minted copper cash, all carefully selected to be of equal size and strung together with bright-red colored cord; every two women carried one table. There were three tables in all. Lin Zhixiao's wife directed them to place two below the tables of Aunt Xue and Aunt Li and to carry the remaining one beneath Grandmother Jia's couch. “Just leave it there on the floor,” said Grandmother Jia. These women all knew the household rules well. After setting down the tables, they unfastened all the cash, pulled out the colored cords, and heaped the loose coins upon the tabletops. The performance of “The Meeting in the Tower,” from The Western Tower, was just drawing to an end. After Yu Shuye had stalked off in anger, Wenbao launched into a comic improvisation: “Off you go in a huff! As it happens, today is the fifteenth day of the first month, and the Old Ancestress is holding a family banquet at Rongguo House. The important thing is for me to mount this horse, hurry inside, and beg a few fruits to eat.” At this, Grandmother Jia and the others all burst out laughing. “What a clever little imp!” said Aunt Xue and the others. “The poor dear!” “The boy is only nine,” said Xifeng. Grandmother Jia laughed. “How remarkable that he should put it so cleverly.” Then she uttered the single word, “Reward!” Three of the women already had winnowing baskets prepared. The moment they heard the word “reward,” they stepped forward to the piles of loose cash, scooped up a basketful apiece, and went out toward the stage, calling, “The Old Ancestress, the honored aunts, and the honored in-law lady reward Wenbao so that he may buy himself some fruit!” With that, they scattered the coins over the stage, which rang from end to end with their loud clattering. Jia Zhen and Jia Lian had already ordered the pages to bring large baskets full of cash, which they kept secretly in readiness nearby. When they heard Grandmother Jia grant a reward—but to learn exactly what followed, read the next chapter.
